english:
From a single individual one may conclude regarding all individuals of the same species and learn that each of its individuals has such a form[^4]. In saying this, my aim is to establish that from the form of one of the relations of the prophets[^1], thou mayest conclude regarding all other relations of the same species.

[^4]: In other words: By examining a single individual of any species, and by recognizing that which constitutes its essential form or *quiddity*, one concludes, by induction, that all individuals of the same species have the same quiddity. — The word צורה̈ designates here *a specific form*, and it is wrongly that Ibn-Tibbon has rendered it by תכונה, *constitution*. The version of Al-’Harîzi bears: ויוָּדע בי זאת צורת בל איש ממנו.
[^1]: Word for word: *of a single form from among the forms of the relations of the prophets*. The author means, it seems to me, that it suffices to have recognized the form of a certain part of the prophet's relation to conclude regarding all parts of that relation; if one of the parts of the vision related by the prophet is recognized as a parable, all the rest will likewise have a parabolic sense. The sense which I attribute to our passage seems to me to emerge from the following example of a dream in which one believes oneself to be making a journey and where one sees all manner of imaginary details. Each of the examples which the author is about to cite from Ezekiel and other prophets is recognized as a vision by one of the expressions which designate prophetic vision, and henceforth all the details reported by the prophet form part of this same vision.

After this preliminary observation, it must be known that, just as a man believes he sees, in a dream, that he has made a journey to such a country, that he was married there, and that after having remained there a certain time, a son was born to him to whom he gave such a name and who was in such a state and in such a circumstance[^2a], so likewise these prophetic parables which appear to the prophet, or which, in the prophetic vision, are translated into action[^1] [when the parable requires[^2b] any act whatsoever], as well as certain things which the prophet executes, the intervals of time which are mentioned parabolically between the different actions and the translations from one place to another, all this (I say) exists only in the prophetic vision, and these are not real actions existing for the external senses[^3]. Some of these things are reported in the prophetic books in an absolute manner[^4]; for, as soon as it is known that the whole was a prophetic vision, it was unnecessary to repeat at every detail of the parable that it had taken place in the prophetic vision.

[^2a]: Literally: *and it was of his state and of his thing* (or *condition*) *in such and such a manner*. The words כית וכית are found in only one of the mss. which I have been able to consult, and where they have been added by a more recent hand. However, the sense of the sentence requires these words, or another similar expression. The version of Al-’Harîzi appears to express the words כית וכית; it bears: והיה עניינו כך וכך. Ibn-Tibbon translates: והיה מעניינו מה שהיה, which would lead one to suppose that his Arabic copy had מא כאן. Both translators have rendered these two words חאל and אמר, which are nearly synonymous, by the single word עניין. Maimonides had perhaps written: וכאן מן האלה ומן אמרה כדׄלך; the copyists may have omitted the word כדׄלך, because this word was repeated immediately after …. כדׄלך הדׄה אלאמתׄאל.
[^1]: Literally: *which are seen, or which are made, in the prophetic vision, etc.*
[^2b]: The version of Ibn-Tibbon bears: במה שיורה, which is inaccurate. Al-’Harîzi translates: וכל מה שיחייב המשל ההוא ממעשה וכו׳; here the Arabic verb אקתצׄי is rendered exactly by שיחייב; but the words וכל מה are an inaccurate translation of the Arabic words פי מא.
[^3]: The author means that all the details recounted in a prophetic vision, as well as all the acts attributed therein to the prophet, form part of the vision and must not be considered as real facts.
[^4]: That is to say: some of these details are recounted simply and in an absolute manner, without it being expressly said that they belong to the vision, so that the vulgar take them for real facts. — Instead of בעצׄהא, the Leyden ms., no. 18, has בעדה, a reading little plausible, but which was reproduced by Al-’Harîzi: ובא זכרון זה בספרי הנבואה אחר זה במאמר מוחלט. Instead of the adverb מטלקא (mss. מטלק), several mss. have מטלקה̈, an adjective which refers to בעצׄהא; likewise Ibn-Tibbon: קצתם מוחלטים.

Thus, the prophet having said: *And the Lord said unto me*, has no need to declare that it was in a dream[^5]; but the vulgar imagine that these actions, these displacements, these questions and answers, that all this (I say) took place in the state of sense perception[^1], and not in the *prophetic vision*.

[^5]: For, as the author has said above (chap. XLI, p. 314): "Whenever a passage (of Scripture) says of someone that an angel spoke to him, or that the word of God was addressed to him, this could not have taken place otherwise than in a dream or in a prophetic vision." The author here makes allusion to several passages where one finds the formula ויאמר י״י אלי, *and the Lord said unto me*, and where there are attributed to the prophet either actions, or displacements, or discourses with God. See e.g.: Jeremiah, chap. 1, v. 7, 9, 12 and 14; chap. XIII, v. 6 and following; Ezekiel, chap. XLIV, v. 1 and following; Zechariah, chap. 11, v. 13 and following.
[^1]: That is to say, that these are real facts, accomplished by the prophet while his senses were functioning and manifesting all their activity.

I shall cite for thee an example regarding which no one could be mistaken, and I shall attach thereto some other examples of the same species; from these few examples, thou mayest conclude regarding those which I shall not have cited. That which is clear and regarding which no one can be mistaken, is when Ezekiel says: *I sat in mine house, and the elders of Judah sat before me, etc. And a spirit lifted me up between the earth and the heaven, and brought me in the* VISIONS OF GOD *to Jerusalem* (Ezekiel 8:1 and 3). Likewise when he says: *I arose, and went forth into the plain* (ibid., 3:23), this was also only in the *visions of God*, as it is also said concerning Abraham: *And he brought him forth abroad* (Genesis 15:5), which took place *in a vision* (ibid., v. 1). Likewise when he says: *And set me down in the midst of the valley* (Ezekiel 37:1), it was again *in the visions of God*. Ezekiel, in this vision wherein he was introduced into Jerusalem, expresses himself[^2a] in these terms: *I looked, and behold a hole in the wall. Then said he unto me: Son of man, dig now in the wall: and when I had digged in the wall, behold a door* (ibid., 8:7-8). Just as it had seemed to him *in the visions of God* that he was commanded to dig in the wall in order to enter and see what was being done there, and that he subsequently digged, as he says, in these same *visions of God*, entered through the opening and saw what he saw, all this in a prophetic vision, so likewise, when God says to him: *Take thee a tile etc., lie thou also upon thy left side etc. Take thou also unto thee wheat, and barley etc.* (ibid., 4:1, 4 and 9), and likewise again, when He says to him: *And cause it to pass upon thine head and upon thy beard, etc.* (ibid., 5:1), all this signifies that, in a prophetic vision, it seemed to him that he performed the actions which he had been commanded to do. Far be it from God to make His prophets a laughing-stock for fools and an object of mockery[^1], and to command them to perform acts of madness[^2b]! Let us add to this that he would have been commanded to disobey the Law; for, as he was a priest, he would have rendered himself guilty of two transgressions for every corner of the beard or of the hair that he would have cut[^3]. But all this took place only in a *prophetic vision*. Likewise, when it is said: *Like as my servant Isaiah hath walked naked and barefoot* (Isaiah 20:3), this took place only in the *visions of God*. It is only men weak in reasoning who believe that in all these passages the prophet relates that he had been really commanded to do such a thing, and that he did it; thus he would relate that he had been commanded to dig the wall which was on the Temple Mount in Jerusalem, although he was then in Babylon, and he would add that he really digged it, as he says: *And I digged in the wall* (Ezekiel 8:8). However, he says expressly that this took place in the *visions of God*.

[^2a]: The verb קאל is a pleonasm which uselessly repeats the verb ודׄכר. Ibn-Tibbon has not translated the verb קאל.
[^1]: Most of our mss. bear: צׄחכה̈ ללספהא וסכׄריה̈, and it is this reading which the version of Al-’Harîzi expresses, which bears: לעג לרקים והתול. Instead of צׄחכּה̈, *laughing-stock*, some mss. have הָדָא, *a target*, a reading which Ibn-Falaquéra also had, who critiques Ibn-Tibbon for having put in his version: דומים לשוטים ולשכורים (see Appendix to the *Moré ha-Moré*, p. 156). It is not understood whence Ibn-Tibbon took the word דומים, *similar*. As for the word ולשכורים, Ibn-Falaquéra observes that instead of סכׄריה̈ (سُخْرِيَّة) or סכׄרה̈ (سخرة), which signifies *laughing-stock* (לעג וקלם), Ibn-Tibbon read סכרה̈, with a כ without a point, that is to say سكرة, plural of شكر
